[主题] Rechargeable aids: wanted by customers or by factories? (173帖 4512览)
[我方 #175]
Factory side here, we build OTC aids in China for other brands. Nobody in 173 posts has been on the manufacturing end of this, so rather than re-argue the preference I’d rather answer the two things that got left open. user_119 is right in #22 and that’s worth saying plainly. The top DSP platform being rechargeable only is a product decision, not a physics limit. We do the same thing. When you segment a lineup, the feature that costs nothing to withhold is the one that ships on the newer housing, and the newer housing is sealed. So people who want the best processing get moved to rechargeable whether or not they ever wanted to leave batteries. Calling that a customer preference is doing a lot of work. Where the mechanism usually gets told wrong is the current argument. It isn’t average draw. A 312 runs a modern DSP perfectly well. What it struggles with is the peak while the LE Audio radio is transmitting, because zinc air has high internal impedance and the voltage sags under bursts. You can engineer around that with a 675 and more bulk capacitance. Which is david.hendon’s question in #77 , whether anyone actually knows if it could be made to work. It could. A 675 aid with a de rated streaming profile is buildable today. It doesn’t get built because the volume isn’t there to pay for a separate housing tool, and housing tooling is where the money goes. The part I should hand over rather than wait to be asked about is the battery door. It’s the most expensive piece of the shell. A hinge, two contacts and a hole through the case. It’s the single biggest leak path for an IP rating and it’s a large share of mechanical warranty returns. Delete it and the factory gains a sealing spec, loses a failure mode and drops an assembly step. So the honest answer to the thread title is both, and the factory half of that is real and it isn’t small. And the cost of it lands on the buyer in a way that mostly gets left out here. A sealed cell has an end date. Around year four or five it wants replacing as a paid service, and on older platforms that service quietly stops being offered, at which point something repairable has become something replaceable. user_119 has the direction of the incentive right even where the mechanism was off. On the disaster case that opened this thread, since it never really got answered: most charger cases only hold two or three full charges in reserve, so the case on its own isn’t the answer. What does answer it is that nearly all of them take USB, so anything that makes 5V keeps you going, a power bank, a car socket, a small panel. The other side is worth knowing too. Zinc air cells have a shelf life of roughly three to four years sealed, so a stockpile isn’t open ended either. Both routes have an edge, they just sit in different places. Happy to be checked on any of it.

draft:
Thirteen is the better answer than 675 and you're right to push me there. A 13 cell holds up under the streaming peaks well enough, and a 13 housing is barely larger than a 312 one while being smaller than most rechargeables once you count the sealed cell. If anyone were going to build the thing, that's the size they'd build it in.

On the tooling being peanuts, you're right and my wording sent you the wrong way. When I said most expensive piece of the shell I meant its share of the shell bill of materials, not that anyone can't afford it. A housing tool is tens of thousands of dollars. For these companies that's a rounding error and it would be dishonest of me to hide behind it.

What actually keeps the variant from existing is what follows the tool, and it's annual rather than one off. Every housing variant becomes a separate line in the fitting software, its own firmware validation matrix, its own regulatory file in every market you sell in, its own spare parts, its own repair flow, its own slot in the dispenser catalogue. None of that is expensive either. It's just permanent, and it has to be justified every planning cycle by a volume number that keeps shrinking.

Then the catalogue finishes it off. Dispensers stock what moves. Once the battery version drops below some share, it comes off the order form, and after that nobody can buy it, which shows up next year as proof nobody wanted it.

So the honest version isn't that it costs too much. It's that nobody inside these companies has a target that gets better by keeping the battery version alive, and plenty have targets that get better by cutting SKUs. That's a worse answer than expense, because expense you could argue with.

[Quora 问题] How do hearing aid brands fit Bluetooth into a hearing aid?
[话题] Hearing Aid Brands · Bluetooth Devices · Assistive Technologies · Hearing Aid Technology · Hearing Aid Industry
[最近活动] 2025-08

[现有答案1] Paul Dudley (50 years as an audiologist, retired, 4y): To the best of my knowledge, they don't, because a Bluetooth receiver can't be made small enough. They use an intermediate step: a gadget you wear on a neckloop or something similar, that incorporates a Bluetooth receiver and a transmitter using a different proprietary short-range technology to transmit the signal to the hearing aid. In my days as an audiologist, I fitted a few clients with a system like this, and I used to wear one myself; it worked fine.

[现有答案2] Ed King (Medical Practice Administrator/Audiology practice, 4y): I'd respectfully disagree with Paul Dudley. I'm wearing a pair of hearing aids with bluetooth and NO additional apparatus around the neck. Our practice has sold these types of hearing aids from a wide variety of major manufacturers for the past 7-8 years at least. You can look on the websites of any manufacturer and see the universal Bluetooth logo for their various models. I can listen to podcasts, hear audiobooks, take phone calls hands free (answering the caller by just speaking since the hearing aid will pick up my voice) and get remote adjustments.
draft:
Paul's answer was correct when he wrote it, and the reason it stopped being correct is worth knowing, because it wasn't size.

The neckloop streamers existed because of current, not because a radio couldn't be made small. Classic Bluetooth pulls tens of milliamps while it transmits. A zinc air cell in a hearing aid can supply roughly one milliamp continuously, and it sags badly under bursts because its internal resistance is high. So the streamer carried its own lithium cell, ran Bluetooth on that, and relayed to the aids over a proprietary near field magnetic link that costs almost nothing to receive. Paul fitted those, and they worked, and the physics behind them hasn't changed.

What changed was two things arriving together. Bluetooth Low Energy dropped the transmit duty cycle far enough that a hearing aid battery could carry it, and the chipmakers put the radio on the same die as the sound processing instead of beside it. Once the radio stops being a separate component with its own power budget, it stops needing its own body to live in.

The antenna is the part people never guess. At 2.4 GHz a quarter wave antenna wants about 31 millimetres, which no ear level device has. So there isn't a real antenna in there. There's a folded trace, or a loop routed around the inside of the shell, or the receiver wire pressed into service as a radiator. Efficiency is poor by any normal standard. It only works because the phone is a metre away and both ends know it.

That leaves four different ways manufacturers actually did it, and it explains why compatibility is such a mess. Apple licensed a proprietary profile to manufacturers under NDA. Google shipped its own, ASHA. Phonak went the other way and put real Classic Bluetooth in the aid, which is why theirs pair with anything and why they run a bigger battery. And now LE Audio is meant to replace all three.

The neckloop never actually died either. It just moved. Every TV adapter and remote microphone on the market today is the same relay architecture, doing the same job for the same reason.
